html:
A water tunnel 1,036 metres long through a mountain on the island of Samos, dug in the 6th century BCE to bring spring water to the city. Its engineer was Eupalinos of Megara, and the work was done under the tyrant Polycrates.

Two teams dug from opposite ends of the mountain at once and met in the middle with an error of only a few metres. To do this, Eupalinos had to carry levels and directions over and around the mountain, an early feat of applied geometry. A pipe in a trench along the floor carried the water.

Herodotus counted it among the three greatest works of the Greeks, all on Samos. It is the second known tunnel dug from both ends, after Hezekiah's Tunnel in Jerusalem, and the first where a clear method was used. It was used for about a thousand years and can be visited today. Pythagoras grew up on Samos in the same years.
